accuracy.evidence: Checked against CCSS 6.SP.4 (dot plots, histograms and box plots on a number line), 6.SP.2 and 6.SP.5 (describe centre, spread and overall shape), HSS-ID.A.1, and the KS3 statistics programme of study (grouped frequency tables for continuous data). All histograms use equal class widths, so bar height equals frequency; the adult text flags that unequal widths at GCSE need frequency density. Boundary convention 20 ≤ t < 30 is stated and used consistently.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets reading stack height as the value (height tag, p1 and m5 where 11 is a distractor), treating a gap as an impossible value (impossible tag, prediction in step 2, m1), placing a boundary value in the class that ends there (boundary tag, step 5 question about 30 s, p3), gaps between bars as if data were categorical (space and cat tags, m2), and over-wide classes hiding the shape (wide tag, step 3, m6).

lab_distinct.evidence: flaghist is the only lab that stacks dots on a number line from data cards, asks for peak, gap and outlier taps on that plot, re-bins one data set live at widths 2, 5, 10 and 20 cm, and has bar tops dragged to frequencies. flagdtype only classifies variables and picks a chart type; it never draws or reads a distribution.

lab_teaches.evidence: The steps follow the concept chain: a dot per value, then describing shape with the exact words, then why grouping is needed for many continuous values, then how bars are built from a frequency table, then reading the modal class and a boundary value. Wrong taps explain the reason, such as 30 is the boundary, so 30 s starts the next class.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions with plausible wrong options: which value will be the tallest stack before plotting, whether a gap means an impossible value, what 20 cm classes do to the shape, and why bars touch (save space is the common wrong answer). Each reveal comes after the student has seen the evidence in the lab.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five rotating questions with three tagged options each; each wrong option gets a targeted reason, for example choosing 6 goals for the peak explains that 6 is the number of dots in the stack and the peak is the value under it, and choosing both classes for t = 20 explains that a value counted twice would break the total.

readability.evidence: Learner paragraphs define each term in plain words with a concrete example (ten football matches, 300 heights, 149.9 cm against 150 cm) and short sentences suited to ages 11 to 13. Adult paragraphs use the precise vocabulary: distribution, class interval, class width, class boundary, modal class, frequency density, discrete and continuous.

no_filler.evidence: Each paragraph adds a new idea: dot plot and mode, shape words, why and how to group, why bars touch and class width, then curriculum, vocabulary, specific mistakes, and the lab route. Items cover mode, number of classes, boundaries, totals, gaps, outliers, modal class and width choice without repeating one another.

mobile.evidence: On iPhone 13 in light and dark the 23-column travel-time plot labels every second value so numbers do not collide, histogram labels thin out when there are many edges, the width chips fit in one row, and each canvas action has a button row underneath (values, widths, bar select and plus or minus, class buttons).

accessibility.evidence: Every tap or drag has a labelled button (Put the dot at 2 goals, Class width 5 cm, Raise the 20–30 bar, Pick the 30–40 second class); results are announced through the live status and canvas aria-label; axe passes in both themes; colours come from the theme palette, and correctness is also stated in words, not colour alone.

sources: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 6 Statistics and Probability 6.SP.2, 6.SP.4, 6.SP.5 and High School S-ID.A.1
National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study, Key Stage 3 Statistics (DfE, 2013)
